The video opens with a black screen displaying white text that serves as a disclaimer. The text specifies that the video is for educational purposes only and not for commercial use. It also states that the video is under the Creative Commons Attribution license and that any reuse must attribute the work to "Labs for Life," a partnership project of MoHFW and CDC. Additionally, it includes an acknowledgment of various medical institutions. The scene then transitions to a dark blue screen, where the title "Hemoglobin by Cyanmethemoglobin Method, Learning Objectives" appears in white text at the top. Underneath the title, a bulleted list outlines the video's highlights: "Principle, Procedure, Quality control, Result interpretation." The video subsequently fades out into a dark blue background with a yellow colored text saying “Hb Estimation by Cyanmethemoglobin Method” and moves to a bullet point saying “Internationally recommended method for determining hemoglobin” in yellow color.

The video segment features a screen displaying information about the Hb estimation by the Cyanmethemoglobin method. On the screen is the title “Hb Estimation by Cyanmethemoglobin Method” in yellow. Below the title is “Principle” in teal. Underneath that, it says “Blood + Reagent solution (Potassium cyanide and potassium ferricyanide)”. Under that is “Converts Hb to methemoglobin” with a down arrow pointing to “Cyanmethemoglobin”. Another arrow points down to “Absorbance is measured in”. This information outlines the principle behind the Cyanmethemoglobin method, detailing that blood combined with a reagent solution containing potassium cyanide and potassium ferricyanide converts hemoglobin to methemoglobin, which then transforms into cyanmethemoglobin, the absorbance of which is measured. The screen has a dark blue gradient background with a textured border. The scene remains static without any people or visual changes.

The video segment illustrates the method of Hemoglobin (Hb) Estimation by Cyanmethemoglobin method. This scene begins with a slide titled "Hb Estimation by Cyanmethemoglobin Method," with a flow chart explaining the principle behind it: mixing blood with a reagent solution (potassium cyanide and potassium ferricyanide) converts Hb to methemoglobin and then to cyanmethemoglobin. The slide indicates that absorbance can be measured with a spectrophotometer at a wavelength of 540 nm or with a colorimeter using a yellow-green filter. This transitions into a slide listing necessary equipment, namely a micropipette and a colorimeter or spectrophotometer. The text highlights that the principle applied for hemoglobin estimation is the same in both devices, but the wavelengths available for estimation differ. Finally, the slide shifts to a slide titled "Reagents required," to provide a listing of the supplies needed to preform the Hb estimation.

The video segment begins with a slide labeled "Hb Estimation by Cyanmethemoglobin Method: Reagents required," showing a white bottle on a white surface, labeled "Drabkin's solution." Next to this is the text “pH of the solution-7.0-7.4” and “Unstable if exposed to light." Then the image switches to a brown bottle with the words “Drabkin Solution” on it. The last bit of text reads, "Stored at room temperature in brown borosilicate bottles." Finally, the image changes to a test tube, which has a clear, pale yellow liquid inside. Next to this is the text “Solution should be clear and pale yellow in color." After this, there is a gloved hand that places a test tube of pale yellow liquid into a machine that is labeled “ELICO CL 223 COLORIMETER”. The machine display shows “CAL 54”, and the hand pushes the "ST" button, which causes the display to change to "0.00 54." The speaker mentions the machine being set to a wavelength of 540 NM. Finally, the video ends with the slide “Hb Estimation by Cyanmethemoglobin Method: Reagents required."

The video segment centers around reagents required for Hb Estimation by the Cyanmethemoglobin Method. The slide is titled "Hb Estimation by Cyanmethemoglobin Method" and "Reagents Required" displayed in teal text. On the left side of the slide is a framed photograph of a white plastic bottle filled with Drabkin's solution on top of white paper. To the right of the image is written, "Room temperature > 30°C then store in refrigerator but brought to room temperature before use." Beneath it is written, "Discard the solution" followed by bullet points that read "Turbid," and "pH is outside range" and "Do not pipette solution by mouth." The scene transitions to an image of an gloved hand holding a bottle with a red cap that reads "Hb Standard solution." A bullet point beneath the image reads, "Available commercially at a specific concentration." The background is a gradient dark blue.

The video displays a static image related to "Hb Estimation by Cyanmethemoglobin Method." The title text is at the top of a blue background. The main focus is on a small, brown glass bottle with a red cap labeled "Hemoglobin Test H.G. Standard 10 ml." The bottle is held by a hand wearing a white glove. Below the bottle, the text "Hb Standard solution" is present. To the right of the bottle, there's a list of "Reagents required," with the following points: "Available commercially at a specific concentration," "Stored in a brown bottle as it is photosensitive," "Exposure to light causes deterioration in the strength of the standard," and "The concentration of the standard used in this demonstration is 14.8 gm% (Derivation of this number will be discussed later)." This indicates that the video is explaining the requirements for the Cyanmethemoglobin method for Hb estimation, emphasizing the need for a specific concentration of a commercially available, photosensitive standard hemoglobin solution stored in a brown bottle.

Two images are shown, the first shows a test tube rack holding a test tube with a purple cap, and the text beneath says "Venous blood in EDTA tube". The second image shows a person wearing white gloves pricking someone's finger, and the text beneath says "Capillary blood by finger prick", followed by "Sample". The video then displays the word "Procedure" in teal against a dark blue background. The scene shifts to someone wearing a printed dress and white gloves using a pipette to extract Drakin's solution from a white bottle into several test tubes. Once the tubes are filled, the person removes a test tube of venous blood with a purple cap, gently inverts the tube to mix the sample, draws 0.02 ml of blood into a pipette, and wipes the outside of the pipette with a tissue. Finally, the person places the pipette into the test tube of Drakin's solution and slowly expels the blood into the solution, mixing it well. The segment ends with the completed tubes resting in the metal rack.

The video segment opens with a dark blue screen displaying the title "Hb Estimation by Cyanmethemoglobin Method". Below this, in smaller text, is "Preparation of Standard curve for Hemoglobin estimation by Cyanmethemoglobin method". The screen then lists several factors when a new calibration curve must be prepared: "Test method", "Colorimeter", "Cuvette type", and "Reagent lot" next to each other in purple, followed by "Is changed" in salmon text. The screen transitions to show the word "Advantages", followed by a list: "All forms of Hb except sulfhemoglobin are converted to cyanmethemoglobin," "Visual error is eliminated as no color matching is required," and "A reliable and stable reference standard is available from WHO." The screen again transitions to show the word "Disadvantages", followed by a list of these: "Potassium cyanide is a poisonous substance," "The rate of conversion of blood containing carboxyhemoglobin is slowed considerably," "Abnormal plasma proteins cause turbidity," and "High leucocyte count causes turbidity on dilution of blood." The screen then lists out reference ranges of Hemoglobin estimation by Cyanmethemoglobin Method for different ages and sexes. The final screen gives credit to a cooperative agreement between U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the Department of Health and Human Services.
